title: Cascading impacts of Atlantic meridional overturning circulation weakening and collapse on marine biogeochemistry
abstract: Abstract As anthropogenic emissions continue to increase Earth’s surface temperature, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is at risk of weakening substantially and crossing a tipping point. Then, multiple Earth system components may be significantly and irreversibly altered. Here we investigate the responses of ocean carbon uptake, net primary productivity (NPP), oxygen concentration, and carbon storage to an AMOC collapse induced by extremes in the internal variability in the subpolar gyre under a moderate forcing scenario. While similar ensemble splitting has been found in other models, the NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS) Earth system model (ESM) was the first to report an AMOC bifurcation due to internal variability, without the need to prescribe freshwater hosing. We find severe regional impacts, including collapsed NPP and deoxygenation in the subpolar North Atlantic, and reduced carbon uptake in the Arctic and subtropical North Atlantic. We identify the physical drivers of these ocean biogeochemical impacts and, for the first time, provide estimates of their lag and latency, i.e. the timescales over which these impacts begin to occur and are fully realized, respectively. Timescales are generally found to increase southward from the deep convection sites, but are remarkably similar between basins at similar latitudes.

title: Evaluating ice shelf basal melt rates in the Southern Ocean high-resolution model against satellite remote sensing
abstract: Ice shelf melt rates by a warm ocean have a critical impact on ice sheet mass balance in Antarctica and in turn on the rates of sea level rise. Validating and tuning modeled ice shelf melt rates is a challenge. Here we discuss the issues by presenting validation of melt rates calculated from the Southern Ocean high-resolution model (SOhi) over the year 2007. SOhi includes full physics, tides, and an updated bathymetric compilation. We compare the model results to two satellite-derived estimates. Overall, we find that the model overestimates ice shelf melt, which we attribute to the ocean model initial (warm) conditions in some areas, bathymetric uncertainties in others, simplified physics on some ice shelves, and also to the inherent limitations of the satellite-derived estimates. The SOhi model nevertheless provides a comprehensive, detailed mapping of ice shelf melt rates around Antarctica; it captures higher melt near grounding lines and ice fronts, areas of freezing versus areas of high melt water production. The identified discrepancies between model and satellite-estimates provide guidelines for model improvements, requirements for additional observations of ice shelf cavities, and assembling of calibration/validation datasets to constrain the models.

title: Radiative effects of decreased North America and European aerosols weaken the AMOC via wind-driven freshwater advection
abstract: Abstract Growing observational and modeling evidence suggests that the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) has weakened since the 1980s, with reductions in North American and European (NAEU) aerosols identified as a potential contributing factor. Here we use fully coupled climate model experiments to demonstrate that the radiative forcing associated with decreased NAEU aerosols weakens the AMOC by enhancing freshwater transport from the Arctic and subtropical regions into the deep convection region. Reduced aerosol loading induces large-scale atmospheric circulation adjustments, including cyclonic wind stress anomalies over the Arctic Ocean and the subtropical North Atlantic. Over the Arctic Ocean, the cyclonic wind stress anomaly weakens the Beaufort Gyre, releasing freshwater that accumulates north of the Canadian Arctic Archipelago and Greenland. This freshwater is then exported through Baffin Bay into the Labrador Sea, suppressing deep convection there. Simultaneously, enhanced cyclonic wind stress over the subtropical North Atlantic weakens the North Atlantic Current (NAC), reducing the northward transport of saline water and promoting the freshwater accumulation within the subpolar gyre. This freshwater anomaly is then advected toward the Labrador Sea, further suppressing deep convection and weakening the AMOC. Together, our results identify a remotely driven pathway through which reductions in NAEU aerosols weaken the AMOC via wind-driven freshwater advection. The robustness of this mechanism is further supported by the multi-model ensemble mean from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) simulations, which exhibits consistent oceanic and atmospheric circulation responses.

title: SURFACE OCEANOGRAPHIC VARIABILITY DURING THE LAST GLACIAL MAXIMUM AND LATE HOLOCENE IN THE INDONESIAN MARITIME CONTINENT
abstract: This study provides a statistical characterization of surface oceanography in the Indonesian Maritime Continent (IMC) during the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM; 23–19 ka) and Late Holocene (LH; 4–0 ka). Using the lgmDA v2.1 paleoclimate data assimilation product, we analyze sea surface temperature (SST), sea surface salinity (SSS), and seawater $\delta^{18}$O. Results indicate the LGM was significantly cooler, saltier, and isotopically enriched, with reduced spatial heterogeneity compared to the LH. Comprehensive nonparametric testing confirms these differences reflect fundamental changes in distributional properties, not merely mean-state shifts. The findings suggest a major oceanographic regime shift, likely driven by lower sea levels, a weakened ITF, enhanced stratification, and a drier regional climate during the LGM. This work offers a statistical framework for understanding IMC sensitivity to glacial-interglacial forcing.

title: North Atlantic response to a quasi-realistic Greenland meltwater forcing in eddy-rich EC-Earth3P-VHR hosing simulations
abstract: Abstract. The vast majority of studies examining the impact of freshwater from ice sheet melting on the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) use climate models that cannot resolve mesoscale ocean processes and do not include an accurate spatio-temporal distribution of the freshwater forcing. These two factors critically affect the nature of the AMOC response. Our study fills that gap with a set of three hosing experiments performed with the global configurations of the eddy-rich climate model EC-Earth3P-VHR. The model is forced for 21 years with a spatial and monthly distribution of Greenland meltwater fluxes derived from observations, equal to 0.04 Sv on an annual average. Within the first year, we observe a response of reduced salinity in the Greenland and Labrador currents. This is accompanied by an acceleration and a cooling along the currents that lead to a rapid weakening of the AMOC at subpolar latitudes. Around year 7, deep mixing in the Labrador Sea begins to weaken due to as freshwater anomalies accumulate through lateral exchanges with the boundary currents. This shallowing of the mixed layer further weakens the AMOC, resulting in a stronger reduction that reaches also the subtropical latitudes. By the end of the simulation, the AMOC has weakened by almost 3 Sv at subppolar latitudes (i.e. a decrease of around 20 %), with an average relative decrease of 10 % for the whole Northern Hemisphere. The reduction in the AMOC is strong enough for some global climate impacts to emerge, such as the “bipolar seesaw” temperature response.

title: Seasonal icings reveal subsurface water drainage of a Greenland Ice Sheet outlet glacier
abstract: Ice cores from Isunnguata Sermia’s forefield reveal how proglacial naled and accreted ices form in Greenland. Naledi build up in winter from precipitation and mineral-rich subglacial water, while accreted ice forms in summer through supercooled water upwelling. Geophysical surveys indicate both are fed by subsurface flows potentially originating from the glacier bed. Here, we present the first conceptual model of these formations in Greenland.

title: Persistent bistability of Nordic Seas overflow waters over 800,000 years
abstract: The stability of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a major uncertainty in projections of future climate. However, direct evidence for AMOC tipping behavior on orbital timescales remains scarce. Here, we reconstruct the strength of Iceland-Scotland Overflow Water, a key lower branch of the deep Atlantic circulation, over the past 800,000 years by combining 12 current-speed records from North Atlantic sediment cores with a data-driven hybrid model. The resulting reconstruction reveals persistent alternation between weak (glacial) and strong (interglacial) circulation modes, pervasive millennial-scale variability within both regimes, and systematic asymmetry between weak-to-strong recoveries and strong-to-weak collapses. Threshold and phase-space analyses show that regime shifts occur within a narrow window of atmospheric carbon dioxide and sea level and often follow hysteresis-like loops. Although bistability persists throughout the last 800,000 years, its sensitivity and timing evolve through time. These findings provide long-term, high-resolution, data-driven constraints on the bistability of Nordic Seas overflow waters and its implications for AMOC resilience in a warming world.

title: Glacial abrupt transitions in ocean circulation were much slower than ice-core records imply
abstract: Dansgaard-Oeschger (DO) events during the last ice age are thought to reflect rapid shifts in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). Greenland ice cores suggest warming transitions within only a few decades—or even just over 10 years. Using precisely dated speleothem oxygen-isotope records from the Asian monsoon region, we have shown that the same DO warmings unfolded over more than a century. Isotope modeling revealed that Greenland records primarily capture a rapid atmospheric reorganization triggered by the initial sea-ice retreat in the northeastern North Atlantic, whereas the parallel AMOC recovery and hemispheric thermal adjustment proceeded much more slowly. These findings reveal that natural AMOC transitions evolved more slowly than the rapid North Greenland oxygen-isotope shifts would imply, thereby refining our understanding of “abruptness” during DO events.

title: The rise and fall of a volcanic plateau: Landscape evolution at the fringes of the former Patagonian Ice Sheet, Meseta Chile Chico, central Patagonian Andes
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding Earth‐surface processes along the fringes of large ice sheets is integral to deciphering cold‐region environmental variability and anticipating slope instability under climate change. We investigate the Meseta Chile Chico, a volcanic plateau in the central Patagonian Andes, located at the eastern margin of the former Patagonian Ice Sheet. Here, glacier retreat patterns are well‐constrained, while the influence of periglacial, paraglacial, and postglacial processes is not. We employ geomorphological mapping integrated with geological and palaeoclimate reconstructions to provide a spatio‐temporal model of landscape evolution. Enhanced erosion since the late Pliocene, caused by differential tectonic uplift and glacial isostatic rebound, produced the rugged morphology that characterizes the Meseta Chile Chico. During the Last Glacial Maximum, glaciers occupied surrounding valleys, while the surface of the plateau was reshaped by long‐lasting periglacial freeze‐thaw cycles and nivation. Postglacial landscape adjustment included intensified landslide activity along the edges of the plateau (linked to paraglacial de‐buttressing at its bordering valleys) and regional base‐level changes. During the Holocene, flow‐type landslides became increasingly controlled by climatic variability. The geomorphology of the Meseta Chile Chico reflects an interplay between inherited geology, (de)glaciation, and climate, highlighting the importance of an interdisciplinary approach for understanding recent landscape dynamics in deglaciating mountain regions.

title: Transition to a much warmer climate for the global ocean and Antarctic Ice Sheet coupled system, and its reversibility
abstract: How the Antarctic ice sheet responds to rapid ocean warming remains uncertain. To explore this, we used a coupled ocean–ice sheet model. We compared simulations under present-day conditions with simulations under strong future warming for 50 years, then returned to today's climate. The ocean warmed quickly but recovered within decades. In contrast, several ice streams continued to retreat for centuries. This shows that even brief warming could cause lasting ice loss and sea-level rise.

title: Forçamento orbital e assimetria hemisférica da insolação no pleistoceno-holoceno
abstract: This study models the seasonal and latitudinal redistribution of orbital insolation for five Pleistocene-Holocene periods: MIS 11 (~400 ka), the Last Interglacial (~125 ka), the Last Glacial Maximum (~21 ka), the early Holocene (~11.7 ka), and the present (0 ka BP = 1950 CE), across nine latitudes from 65°S to 65°N. ORBIT91 parameters were used to calculate Earth-Sun distance, solar declination, photoperiod, and daily top-of-atmosphere insolation. At 65°N during the June solstice, Q ranged from 466.0 W m⁻² in MIS 11 to 537.4 W m⁻² in the Last Interglacial. During austral summer, however, the present has the highest value among the analyzed periods at 40°S, 60°S, and 65°S; at 65°S it reaches 510.9 W m⁻², about 7% above the present-day peak at 65°N. The current precessional configuration, with perihelion near the December solstice, explains this asymmetry. The caloric summer metric, surface-energy scenarios, and comparison with FAO-56 complement the analysis. The results frame insolation as a seasonal forcing capable of modulating hemispheric energy contrasts, whose climatic expression depends on atmospheric circulation and Earth-system feedbacks. The transmittance and evaporation scenarios represent idealized energy bounds rather than observed or reconstructed surface-climate conditions.

title: Latitudinal Heterogeneity in South Asian Monsoon Changes Since the Last Glacial Maximum Revealed by Ganga–Brahmaputra Vegetation Record
abstract: Abstract Future changes in South Asian climate are expected to amplify flooding and drought, yet the spatial and temporal variability of the South Asian monsoon (SAM) under different climate regimes remains poorly constrained. Here, we present a new marine pollen record from the Bay of Bengal (BoB), informing on the vegetation of the Ganges‐Brahmaputra (G‐B) River basin whose outlet via the lower Meghna lies near 21.3°–21.8°N, and compare it with bulk and leaf‐wax δ 13 C and δD, and planktonic foraminiferal δ 18 O records, all from the same site. The G‐B basin was characterized by an open landscape with sparse subtropical trees during Marine Isotope Stage (MIS) 2 indicating drier and colder conditions. This is in sharp contrast with the development of tropical forests during MIS 1. During the Holocene, changes in the forest composition, characterized by a progressive increase in dry tropical trees relative to moist taxa, showed large‐scale drying, with more pronounced winter dryness after 8 ka. The comparison with the pollen records located off Mahanadi (20°N) and Godavari (18°N) catchments, both within the Indian core monsoon zone reveals that the composition of the forests differs strongly, showing a persistent north–south hydroclimate gradient. At orbital time scales, vegetation records from the western BoB support that the SAM variability is intrinsically linked to the ITCZ migration and largely affected by the Northern hemisphere ice‐sheets and insolation forcing; this is particularly significant for the Holocene. However, the spatial heterogeneity of hydroclimate conditions suggests additional modulation by Himalayan orography, and vegetation through moisture recycling.

title: Delayed seasonal march of East Asian summer monsoonal rain belt during Heinrich Stadials
abstract: Abstract The timing and duration of monsoon rainfall shape regional hydroclimate, yet their response to abrupt climate change remains poorly constrained. Here, we use 25-km-resolution climate simulations to investigate the seasonal migration of the East Asian summer monsoon rain belt during Heinrich Stadials, periods associated with collapsed Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (AMOC). We find that the rain belt migrated northward 18 days later than during interstadials. This delay kept the monsoon front longer over central China, prolonging early-summer rainfall despite an overall weaker monsoon. The delayed migration was linked to later northward advances of the western North Pacific subtropical high and upper-level westerly jet. North Atlantic cooling contributed to these circulation changes through Rossby wave propagation and a weakened land–sea thermal contrast. Our results suggest that abrupt Atlantic changes can reshape both the amount and seasonal timing of East Asian summer rainfall. These findings offer a palaeoclimate perspective on potential changes in monsoon seasonality under future AMOC weakening.

title: Imaging the Ross Ice Streams of West Antarctica using active source seismology
abstract: Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) Knowledge of the past and future of Earth's ice sheets requires us to image beneath the ice surface and into the ice, water, sediment, and rock that lies beneath. An effective way of doing this uses active source seismology. Here we present active source seismic data imaging a diverse range of subglacial environments including subglacial lakes, sub-ice ocean cavities, and geological archives preserving the history of the ice sheets.

title: Climate variability and human adaptation in late quaternary Northeast Asia: A critical review of paleoenvironmental and archaeological records from Northeast China and Primorye of Russia
abstract: Northeast China and Russian Primorye lie at the confluence of the East Asian summer monsoon, Siberian High, and Pacific maritime circulation. The region experienced pronounced glacial-interglacial variability and served as a corridor for human dispersal among Siberia, East Asia, and the Americas. This review synthesises palaeoecological and archaeological evidence, principally from the past ca. 50 ka. Environmental records trace a transition from the cold, arid steppe of the Last Glacial Maximum (ca. 26.5–19.0 ka BP) to warmer, more forested Holocene landscapes, while revealing strong spatial heterogeneity and abrupt events. Although the ≥146 ka Harbin cranium predates the main review interval, it establishes a Middle Pleistocene hominin presence; securely dated archaeological sequences considered here begin in the Late Pleistocene. These records document developments from Upper Palaeolithic lithic industries to Neolithic sedentism, millet agriculture, and Bronze Age sociopolitical complexity. A central limitation is the spatial separation of most palaeoclimatic archives and archaeological sites. Their differing chronological resolution further restricts direct causal attribution, leaving many proposed climate-culture relationships as working hypotheses. We therefore advocate co-located multiproxy transects, improved chronological control, and tephrochronological correlation. A site-by-site appraisal of radiocarbon, OSL, and U-series chronologies identifies relationships that are currently testable. The Boisman-Krounovka sequence suggests that resource breadth and specialisation may mediate vulnerability to environmental change, although the roles of social organisation, mobility, and demography remain unresolved. Northeast Asia thus offers a framework for generating and testing hypotheses about climatic variability, demographic processes, and cultural change rather than demonstrating simple climate-driven causation.

title: Overshoot pathways: reversible biophysical change, irreversible socioeconomic impacts
abstract: Abstract Exceeding global warming of 1.5 °C in the near term is now unavoidable. An overshoot pathway, in which exceedance is followed by decline to or below the threshold through net-negative emissions, is now the only remaining route back to 1.5 °C. Permanent exceedance forecloses the recovery from climate impacts that an overshoot pathway may permit, yet even an overshoot pathway leaves lasting legacies. To characterise the reversibility of temporary overshoot impacts, we propose a three-layer analytical framework distinguishing hazards (with four dimensions: magnitude, duration, rate of exceedance, and rate of decline), biophysical responses (reversible vs persistent change), and socioeconomic outcomes (reversible vs irreversible impact). We introduce the socioeconomic commitment threshold, endogenous to the overshoot trajectory: how much overshoot intensity a system can experience before the losses it accumulates persist after temperatures decline, explained by three mechanisms: non-substitutability, threshold-crossing, and lock-in. A typology linking biophysical persistence with socioeconomic irreversibility illustrates how reversible biophysical change can produce irreversible socioeconomic loss, while persistent biophysical change need not produce irreversible outcomes where adaptive capacity is sufficient. Whether temporary exceedance produces permanent harm is determined primarily by socioeconomic rather than biophysical factors, except where permanent biophysical change exceeds adaptation limits. For systems and communities with low adaptive capacity, overshoot concentrates irreversible legacies even where temperatures subsequently decline, placing equity and justice at the centre of overshoot assessment.

title: Merging Regional Climate Models and Remote Sensing Observations to Better Estimate Mountain Snow Water Equivalent
abstract: Abstract Large‐scale, high‐resolution estimation of snow water equivalent (SWE) in mountainous regions remains challenging. Continental‐scale approaches, including SWE reconstruction and regional climate model (RCM) simulations, are computationally expensive at high resolutions. We present Blender, a variational data assimilation method that improves modeled SWE and snowfall time series by modifying snowpack mass and energy balance while minimizing changes to input precipitation and energy fluxes, subject to remotely sensed snow cover fraction constraints. Blender combines the advantages of RCM simulation and SWE reconstruction and can be applied as a post‐processing step to many gridded snow data sets. We tested Blender at 500 m resolution in the Tuolumne watershed, Sierra Nevada, USA, during water years 2013, 2016, and 2017 (low, average, and high snow accumulation). We tested Blender with prior inputs from an RCM and ERA5‐Land (ERA5L), and evaluated posterior (output) performance using 18 Airborne Snow Observatory (ASO) flights, and compared its performance with the Western United States Snow Reanalysis (WUS‐SR). Blender improved spatial SWE patterns relative to ASO in all years for the RCM prior (RMSEP: 17.2% → 11.5%, R : 0.39 → 0.72) and ERA5L prior (RMSEP: 13.9% → 12.9%, R : 0.003 → 0.59), approaching WUS‐SR performance (RMSEP = 9.5%, R = 0.82). Blender improved snow water storage (SWS) estimates for the RCM prior but not for ERA5L prior, although ERA5L posterior SWS remained reasonably accurate (median absolute error of 27%). Blender provides a flexible and efficient pathway toward higher‐resolution, large‐scale SWE estimation in mountainous regions.

title: Assessing the potential of Individual Foraminifera Analyses (δ18O) to reconstruct variability, seasonality and  extremes in the tropical Indian Ocean
abstract: The Indian Ocean regulates global climate through heat and moisture exchanges. To understand past climate variability, we analyzed oxygen isotopes in individual fossil shells of tiny marine organisms. Combining numerical simulations, we show that shell chemistry reflects seasonal temperature changes driven by both the monsoon and the Indian Ocean Dipole. This opens new perspectives for reconstructing past climate extreme events.

title: Humid periods over western Sahara during the Middle Miocene Climate Transition and their implications on the carbon cycle
abstract: The Middle Miocene expansion of the Antarctic Ice Sheet coincides with major sedimentological changes in Malta. This interval also saw reorganisations in ocean circulation linked to closure of the Mesopotamian Seaway (MSR-events) and perturbations in the carbon cycle (CM events). The final CM event (CM-6), slightly lags the main glacial phase and remains difficult to interpret due to competing mechanisms and conflicting p CO 2 reconstructions. To explore links between cryosphere, circulation, hydroclimate, and the carbon cycle, we present new geochemical records from Malta. Our records show that cryospheric expansion was followed by large, precessionally paced variations in sea-surface salinity and a marked regional increase in biological productivity. The results indicate a shift toward stronger monsoonal influence, delivering enhanced freshwater and nutrient fluxes to the region. This enhanced local biological carbon pump may have acted as a positive feedback to a global CO 2 drawdown. However, any contribution to global CO 2 drawdown remains tentative and cannot be confirmed without contemporaneous high-resolution open-ocean records.

title: Investigating the transition in ice dynamics from a land- to lake-terminating glacier using a simple glacier dynamics model
abstract: As climate change creates new lakes at the front of retreating glaciers, these ice bodies often accelerate and lose mass more quickly. We used a computer model to study this process at an Icelandic glacier. Our results show that thinning ice is the main driver for recent acceleration, with 37 % of the total ice loss resulting from the presence of the lake. These findings imply that as lakes grow globally, glaciers could vanish more rapidly than predicted, enhancing the rate of sea level rise.

title: Regional Arboreal Pollen Input and Its Millennial-Scale Variability Recorded in an Alpine Lake in the Hengduan Mountains, China
abstract: The Hengduan Mountains are a major hotspot for lake-sediment research, but regional vegetation responses to Holocene climate variability remain incompletely understood. Here, we analyzed pollen assemblages and concentrations from Dinggongniang Co (4633 m a.s.l.) to investigate regional vegetation-related changes over the past approximately 4.7 ka. Pollen percentage and concentration analyses were combined with ensemble empirical mode decomposition (EEMD) and Lomb–Scargle spectral analysis. Despite being located above the modern tree line, the lake sediments are dominated by arboreal pollen (89.5%), particularly Pinus, indicating substantial pollen input from lower-elevation forests. Total pollen concentrations were relatively low around 4.2 ka, increased markedly during the Roman Warm Period, and remained relatively elevated during the Medieval Climate Anomaly, suggesting changes in regional arboreal pollen input potentially associated with Asian summer monsoon-related hydroclimatic variability. Furthermore, time-series analyses identified a possible millennial-scale oscillation at approximately 1.3–1.4 ka, broadly consistent with variability documented in North Atlantic and Asian monsoon records. This finding highlights the value of high-altitude lake pollen records for tracing regional arboreal pollen input and suggests possible connections between Asian monsoon variability and broader Northern Hemisphere climate fluctuations. Although chronological uncertainties and multiple factors influencing pollen concentrations introduce some limitations, the observed patterns offer valuable insights into long-term vegetation-related environmental variability in the Hengduan Mountains.

title: The internal variability modulates marine heatwave duration changes by day-to-day ocean memory in the recent decades
abstract: Abstract The duration of marine heatwaves (MHWs) determines the cumulative thermal stress imposed on marine organisms, thereby strongly influencing the severity of ecological consequences. Recently, day-to-day ocean memory, quantified by a first-order sea surface temperature (SST) autocorrelation model, has been found as an effective metric to depict the duration of MHWs, due to its consistent climatological distribution and trends with MHW duration in the observations. However, the relative importance of external forcing and internal variability in modulating the day-to-day ocean memory and, more importantly, its relationship with MHW duration, remain unclear. In this study, we employ 100 ensemble members of CESM2 and 32 CMIP6 models to analyze the roles of external forcing and internal variability in the day-to-day ocean memory and MHW duration. We find that internal variability dominates the trends of day-to-day ocean memory in the recent decades and further modulates the trends of MHW duration, particularly in the tropical oceans. The zonal gradient of SST trends over the tropical Pacific emerges as a key feature of the internal variability. By combining a stochastic climate model framework with a mixed-layer heat budget, we further reveal that ocean mixing and dynamics are the primary processes through which internal variability modulates trends in day-to-day ocean memory, whereas SST-surface heat flux feedback provides a secondary contribution and variations in mixed-layer depth play negligible roles. This study demonstrates that internal variability exerts a considerable influence on MHW duration through its modulation on day-to-day ocean memory, providing crucial evidence and a new perspective for understanding and predicting MHW duration in a warming climate.

title: EnsAI: An Emulator for Atmospheric Ammonia Ensembles
abstract: arXiv:2504.16024v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ensemble-based methods for data assimilation and emissions inversions are a popular way to encode flow-dependency within the model error covariance. While most ensemble methods do not require the use of an adjoint model, the need to repeatedly run a geophysical model to generate the ensemble can be a significant computational burden. In this paper, we introduce EnsAI, a new AI-based ensemble generation system for surface ammonia concentrations. When trained on an ensemble for ammonia generated by the GEM-MACH air quality model, it was shown that the ensembles produced by EnsAI can accurately reproduce the meteorology-dependent features of the original ensemble, while generating the ensemble 3,300 times faster than the original GEM-MACH ensemble. While EnsAI requires an upfront cost for generating the ensemble used for training, as well as the training itself, the long term computational savings can greatly exceed these initial computational costs. When used in an emissions inversion system, EnsAI produced similar inversion results to those in which the original GEM-MACH ensemble was used while using significantly less computational resources.

title: Volcanic impacts on East Asian climate since 1400: insights from climate reconstructions and paleoclimate reanalysis
journal: Geografiska Annaler Series A Physical Geography
abstract: This study analysed volcanic impacts on East Asian temperature and precipitation (wetness/dryness) anomalies and investigated the consistency of climate responses between the REACHES reconstruction and paleoclimate reanalysis product (ModE-RA) from the 15th to 20th centuries. Volcanic events were compiled from the eruption chronology based on ice-core sulphate data, and 10 major eruption events were identified. For each event, the eruption year was designated as t0 and used as the reference year for event alignment. Superposed epoch analysis was applied with a ± 8-year window to compare post-eruption years (t = 0–8) against pre-eruption baselines (t = −8–−1) by a significance t-test. For identifying whether extreme years (percentile thresholds from the top 5%–25% in temperature and precipitation fields) are attributed to volcanic forcing or natural variability, we adopted Bayes’ conditional probabilities and applied an exact binomial test to perform reverse inference. Both datasets showed robust post-eruption cooling signals, the strongest being within t0 +3 years. Precipitation responses were controversial: REACHES revealed overall wetting, whereas ModE-RA suggested drying, indicating a consistent cooling effect of major volcanic eruptions and divergent responses in hydroclimates. Future analysis should focus on the hydroclimatic effects of volcanic eruptions using high-resolution reconstruction data and simulations.

title: Can multi-glacier moraine analysis constrain paleoclimate reconstructions? Evidence from 3D glacier modeling in the Cordillera Real, Bolivia
abstract: Glacier deposits are used to reconstruct past climate, but the same glacier size can result from different mixes of temperature and snowfall. Using numerical glacier simulations in the Bolivian Andes, we explored how to overcome this ambiguity. We show that combining several neighboring glaciers with independent rainfall records partly resolves it, giving temperatures 0.8°C and 1.3°C lower during the Little Ice Age and Early Holocene (~10,000 years ago), respectively.

title: Evaluating the prediction of subgrid eddy kinetic energy from a machine learning model
abstract: arXiv:2611.06539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Global climate model resolution is still too coarse to fully resolve mesoscale processes, therefore subgrid closures are required to approximate the feedback of eddies onto the resolved flow. With high-resolution datasets now readily available, there has been a rapid growth in the use of machine learning to develop new eddy closures that could help reduce model biases and uncertainty. In this work we employ an offline learning approach with a convolutional neural network to predict subgrid eddy kinetic energy ($KE_e$), laying the initial groundwork for a machine-learned scale-aware GEOMETRIC eddy closure for the UK's Earth System Model. We address the question of whether global parameterizations are needed or if regional closures are sufficient by evaluating a number of neural network models through region and feature ablation experiments. ML parameterization models generalize to unseen regions when their training data share similar feature and target distributions with those regions. Models that fail to generalize incur distributional shift, or employ different filtering scales for the true eddy kinetic energy field. When holding out features, there is improvement among the generalizable ML models, with some feature spaces leading to improvements in some regions but degrading performance in others. Generally, power spectral density of $KE_e$ tend to diverge at small scales, though some feature spaces are able to minimize this divergence. Overall, the best performing model trained on all regions achieves time-mean and anomaly R2 scores of R2$\approx 0.95$ and R2$\approx 0.8 - 0.9$, respectively.

title: Holocene Paleoenvironmental Evolution Recorded in Nearshore Deposits from the Zhejiang Coast
abstract: The Zhejiang region preserves a complete evolutionary trajectory from hunter-gatherer to early state-level societies, which offers critical material for examining social complexity. Nevertheless, the lack of continuous, high-quality Holocene paleoenvironmental archives in this area hampers a thorough assessment of the human–environment interaction over time. This study investigates pollen, ostracod, foraminiferal and particle-size proxies to reconstruct regional environmental dynamics from core TQ1 in Taizhou Bay spanning 14.8–0.4 cal ka BP based on AMS 14C dating. Core TQ1 records a transition from predominantly terrestrial influence during the late deglaciation to increasing marine influence during the early Holocene. Based on paleoenvironmental changes, the Holocene can be further divided into three stages. Stage 1 (11.5–8.5 cal ka BP) was characterized by a coastal environment with stronger hydrodynamics; arboreal pollen declined while herbs, ferns and algae increased. Stage 2 (8.5–4.2 cal ka BP) represented the peak transgression with open marine conditions and maximum microfossil abundance, and forest recovery as terrestrial herbs and algae decreased. Stage 3 (4.2–0.4 cal ka BP) shifted back to nearshore shallow-sea conditions, with persistently high arboreal percentages and sustained pollen input from forested terrestrial source areas. The intense paleoenvironmental changes, coupled with the evolutionary processes of ancient cultures in the adjacent areas, provide new evidence for a deeper understanding of regional cultural evolution.

abstract: The geometry and ventilation of upper deep-water masses in the Pacific sector of the Southern Ocean are critical to glacial carbon storage, yet their evolution since the Last Glacial Maximum remains poorly constrained. Here, we present the foraminiferal neodymium isotope composition (ε Nd ) from core MD97-2115 (eastern Chatham Rise, 2160 m water depth), which is located at the present-day boundary between Upper Circumpolar Deep Water (UCDW) and modified North Pacific Deep Water (mNPDW) in the Southwest Pacific, to reconstruct the upper deep-water mass changes since 30 ka. Combining quantitative binary mixing calculations with vertical ε Nd gradients relative to Lower Circumpolar Deep Water, we suggest substantial shifts in the geometry and mixing of UCDW and mNPDW since 30 ka. The variation phases include reduced UCDW influence during 30–20 ka, enhanced UCDW contribution between 20 and 14.3 ka, slightly decreased UCDW during 14.3–11.4 ka, and stable Holocene conditions. The glacial dominance of mNPDW is consistent with basin-wide evidence for enhanced storage of respired carbon in Pacific-sourced deep waters, likely contributing to the maintenance of low atmospheric CO 2 during the glacial period. Crucially, the early rapid increase in UCDW at ∼20 ka preceded the penetration of North Atlantic-sourced water into Southern Ocean and the deglacial CO 2 increase by several millennia, implying a critical role for Antarctic and Southern Ocean processes in establishing the oceanic precondition for glacial termination. During the last deglacial period, the decoupling between our reconstruction and atmospheric CO 2 evolution suggests that water-mass geometry alone is insufficient to drive the full deglacial CO 2 increase, pointing to additional roles for processes such as regional outgassing and variability in air–sea gas exchange efficiency.

title: A Basin‐Wise GLOF Susceptibility Assessment in the Western Himalayas: Integrating Remote Sensing‐ GIS and Multi‐Criteria Decision Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) pose an increasing threat to high mountain environments across the world, especially in the Himalayas where climate change is accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost degradation. This study presents a detailed GLOF susceptibility analysis of the western Himalayas covering five major river basins, ie Satluj, Chenab, Jhelum, Beas, and Ravi by integrating high‐resolution remote sensing data with a multi‐criteria decision‐making approach. A detailed inventory of 1573 glacial lakes was developed using manual delineation of Sentinel‐2A and LISS‐IV images. Forty‐eight potentially dangerous lakes were identified based on size and dam composition. Following the guidelines of NDMA and GAPHAZ, 12 important physical and geomorphic parameters were selected and evaluated using Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) with the addition of Cumulative Weightage Technique (CWT). AHP Analysis indicated that 20 lakes were high hazard, 23 lakes were medium hazard, and five lakes were low hazard. The basin‐wise analysis revealed that Satluj and Chenab are particularly vulnerable owing to the presence of large and fast‐growing lakes. A temporal assessment of 48 selected potentially dangerous lakes from 2000 to 2024 revealed a 115% increase in total lake area, highlighting their rapid expansion under a warming climate. The susceptibility framework was validated using seven historical GLOF events, all of which had hazard scores > 0.7, in agreement with the high susceptibility lakes identified in this study. The study recommends that detailed field investigations be carried out on high‐hazard lakes including bathymetric surveys, assessments of moraine stability, and real‐time monitoring to validate remote sensing findings and to inform early warning systems. This approach offers a transferable and policy‐relevant framework to support GLOF risk mitigation and climate adaptation planning in glacierized regions. This study relies primarily on remote sensing data, and uncertainties in lake identification and the lack of field validation may affect susceptibility classification.

title: Quantifying snowmelt contribution to streamflow using ensemble machine learning and remote sensing
abstract: Abstract Snowmelt plays a vital role in sustaining river flows and regulating water resources in mountain ecosystems, particularly under changing climatic conditions. This study aims to quantify the contribution of snowmelt to streamflow by estimating snow cover and snow water equivalent (SWE) in the Greater Caucasus Basin of Azerbaijan. MODIS and FLDAS remote sensing products were analyzed using the Random Forest machine learning algorithm, with data processed on the Google Earth Engine (GEE) platform to improve prediction efficiency and accuracy. Results show that Random Forest significantly enhanced snow cover estimation compared to satellite data alone. MODIS and FLDAS observations revealed peak snow cover in December 2023 (1,310 km²) and maximum SWE in February 2023 (23 kg/m²). Over the longer period 2013–2023, the highest snow cover was recorded in 2016 (5,052 km²), while peak SWE occurred in 2019 (188.7 kg/m²). These findings indicate a weakening role of snow in regional runoff regulation and water supply, driven by declining snowfall and streamflow. The study demonstrates the value of machine learning for snowpack monitoring and highlights the need for long-term simulations and expanded ground-based networks to improve prediction of peak flow events in mountain basins.

abstract: Northeast China lies on a mid-latitude boundary where small warming can shift snowfall to rain and shorten the snow season, but climate models often simulate snow fields with large regional biases. Here we show that satellite-constrained, 1-km machine-learning emulators project snow-cover duration without directly using modeled snow variables. They relate observed daily snow cover during 2001–2020 to temperature, precipitation, snowfall fraction and terrain, and are driven by bias-corrected climate projections. Snow seasons shorten almost everywhere, with more than 98% of land grid cells agreeing on the sign of change. By 2081–2100, domain-mean snow-cover duration decreases by 42, 64, and 85 days under low-, intermediate- and high-emission pathways, respectively, and areas with fewer than 50 snow days expand from 19% to 99% under high emissions. Snow-season shortening is dominated by loss of late-winter and spring snow persistence, especially at low–middle elevations and along the present rain–snow transition zone. The loss of snow persistence during late winter to spring across Northeast China leads to shorter snow season under global warming, as suggested by bias-corrected CMIP6 climate projections based on Satellite-constrained machine learning framework.

title: Regional climatic change following the Eocene–Oligocene Transition in central northern Tibet
abstract: The Eocene–Oligocene Transition (EOT) constitutes one of the most dramatic climatic changes in the Cenozoic era; it is characterized by global cooling, increasing aridity, extinction of fauna and flora, and a major drop of global sea level. However, how continental settings responded to global climatic change after the EOT event has still received little consideration. Here we report a high-resolution and well-dated terrestrial EOT record from the Tuotuohe Basin (central northern Tibetan Plateau). Sedimentary facies, fossil evidence, new proxy, and climate modeling data suggest a transition from warm and dry to cool and wet climatic conditions ca. 33 Ma, in contrast with other records from the Tibetan Plateau that commonly document drier conditions after the EOT (ca. 34 Ma). Having considered the potential forcing mechanisms, we propose that the Indian monsoon likely expanded into the Tuotuohe Basin after the EOT due to a combination of factors, such as the land-sea pressure gradient caused by the retreat of the Paratethys Sea, tectonic uplift in central northern Tibet and increased cross-equatorial pressure gradients. This study opens new perspectives for paleoclimate model simulations around the EOT that encompasses major environmental reorganizations at the continent scale, such as the Mongolian Re-modeling (faunal turnovers of Paleogene mammals from the Mongolian Plateau) and the Grande Coupure (extinction of a large number of European native mammals).

title: The seasonal, polar-amplified climate response to a latent heat transport forcing
abstract: Abstract Polar amplification is a well-documented phenomenon driven by multiple feedback mechanisms, with latent heat transport (LHT) playing a role that is often underestimated. Although the total atmospheric energy transport into polar regions remains nearly unchanged in warming scenarios, compensating changes in dry static and latent energy transport interact with polar-amplified surface warming: dry static energy transport generally decreases due to a reduction in meridional temperature gradient, while the latent energy transport increases, contributing to polar warming by enhancing moisture. To isolate the impact of LHT changes, we lock the moisture advection in an idealized general circulation model (GCM) and apply it as a forcing. Simulations forced with an increase in LHT, equivalent to that which would be produced by a doubling of CO 2 , consistently demonstrate substantial polar warming, providing a different perspective from the conventional feedback analysis that attributes polar amplification predominantly to the ice-albedo feedback and lapse-rate feedback. The GCM is coupled to a thermodynamic sea ice model, which allows the role of sea ice to be examined by systematically disabling sea ice-LHT interactions. Sea ice loss strongly enhances annual mean polar amplification and wintertime polar warming, and is itself a response to the increase in LHT. We additionally provide a quantitative comparison of different metrics of LHT-induced polar amplification. These findings suggest that diagnostic decompositions, by only quantifying the enhanced LHT into polar regions and neglecting its impact on polar feedbacks, underestimate the role of LHT as a significant driver of polar amplification.

title: A Deep-Learning Framework for the Generalized Emulation of Atmospheric Radiative Transfer at Microwave Frequencies
abstract: arXiv:2611.07094v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents an application of machine learning to the problem of the computational expense of atmospheric radiative transfer calculations from physics-based models. While in recent studies individual emulators have been created that emulate certain radiative transfer schemes for different sensors, we show that a general framework can be applied to emulate the radiative transfer method itself. A fully connected deep neural network has been trained to predict top-of-atmosphere microwave radiances in all-sky conditions over various land, ocean and sea ice surfaces at all frequencies from 1 to 300 GHz, and for all incidence angles from 0 to 65 degrees. The reference models against which the emulator has been trained include an Eddington two-stream radiative transfer model for one-dimensional and pseudo-three-dimensional microwave brightness temperature simulations. This neural network architecture has also been separately trained to reproduce the explicit calculations of the Community Radiative Transfer Model (CRTM) for a single microwave imager. In all cases, the model architecture is successfully able predict microwave brightness temperatures by being trained directly on the optical properties of the atmosphere and surface and therefore directly emulating the radiative transfer method. Compared to the explicit schemes used to produce the training data, the GPU-enabled emulator is able to produce brightness temperature simulations more than three orders of magnitude faster and with a root-mean-squared-error less than 0.0348 K, 0.0531 K, and 0.0246 K against the independent test data for the two Eddington models and CRTM, respectively. Additionally, preliminary training using a full 3D Monte Carlo scheme for high-resolution simulations shows promising results for the application of this method to "exact" radiative transfer methods, and these results are discussed in Section IV.

title: Explainable AI for Geoscientific Regression: Evaluating Sensitivity and Attribution Methods with the Lorenz-63 System and Applications
abstract: arXiv:2608.07406v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) moves from research prototypes to operational tools in Earth system science, trust in its predictions becomes increasingly important. Explainable AI (XAI) offers insight into how AI models make predictions. However, many influential XAI methods were developed or popularised for classification, and their interpretation for regression, which dominates geoscience, is less well established. A central obstacle is the lack of ground truth for judging explanations. We show that, for a dynamical system with known governing equations, matched references can be built directly from the physics. We extend established sensitivity methods to provide physical references for both sensitivity and attribution, separately for methods with implicit and explicit baselines, all computed from the governing equations independently of the network. Applied to an AI emulator of the Lorenz-63 system, these references show that method families answer distinct questions rather than approximating one ``true'' explanation. The emulator's sensitivities and attributions can depart most from their physical references where it forecasts best, so predictive skill is not a substitute for the physical realism of what a model has learned. We then review XAI applications to Earth system regression, organised by method family, extending to issues an idealised system cannot address: computational scalability, strongly correlated high-dimensional predictors, and reliance on expert judgement where no physical reference exists. We also discuss how an XAI method can be mathematically valid yet only partially relevant to a given stakeholder group. We close with future directions and practical recommendations for responsible XAI use in geoscientific modelling and forecasting.

Technical note: Evaluation of snow water equivalent from large-scale land-surface products over Italy
abstract: Abstract. Snow water equivalent (SWE) is a critical hydrological variable for water resource management in mountainous regions, where seasonal snowpacks function as natural reservoirs regulating streamflow and water supply. While high-resolution, observation-constrained regional or national snow products provide reliable daily SWE estimates at fine spatial resolution (less than 1 km), their limited temporal coverage often restricts their use for long-term hydro-climatological studies. Large-scale land-surface products, in which SWE is derived from land-surface model simulations driven by atmospheric reanalyses or regional dynamical downscaling systems, provide multi-decadal coverage, but their reliability may be affected by biases in meteorological forcing, limited topographic representation, and simplified snow process parameterisation, requiring rigorous regional evaluation. This study evaluates the SWE estimates of three large-scale land-surface products, i.e., the global ERA5-Land, the European CERRA-Land, and the Italian VHR-REA_IT, against the national reference dataset IT-SNOW across Italy. The analysis combines grid-scale bias assessment of mean annual SWE and snow cover duration with temporal correlation analysis of daily SWE series, and is complemented by an evaluation of precipitation and temperature biases in each product, providing insight into how each product represents the atmospheric conditions governing snow accumulation and ablation and thereby supporting the interpretation of the identified SWE discrepancies. The results show clear regional differences in product performance, with no single product performing best across all metrics. ERA5-Land shows the strongest temporal correlation with IT-SNOW, but tends to overestimate mean annual SWE and snow cover duration in the Alps. CERRA-Land shows more moderate biases than ERA5-Land in the Italian Alps, but generally underestimates mean annual SWE across most subregions, where autumn and winter precipitation deficits in the forcing limit snow accumulation. Across the Apennines, both ERA5-Land and CERRA-Land tend to underestimate SWE and snow cover duration, particularly in the northern sectors. VHR-REA_IT shows widespread underestimation and the weakest temporal correspondence with IT-SNOW: this may be due to its fully coupled atmosphere–land architecture with no assimilation of meteorological observations. Overall, the results suggest that forcing biases explain a substantial part of the observed SWE discrepancies, although not all of them. This study provides useful insights for the use of SWE estimates from large-scale land-surface products in long-term hydro-climatological assessments over Italy and helps to understand whether the products can be used to evaluate snow dynamics in mountainous regions lacking high-quality benchmark estimates.

title: Shifts in Rossby wave regimes via the change of group velocity with zonal jets
abstract: arXiv:2611.05922v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evidences show it is questionable to use the trends in Rossby wave phase speed (Cpx) to interpret the relation between the changes of extreme events and westerly jets. We propose, by using 70 years (1954-2023) of ERA5 reanalysis, that the trends in extremes are associated with the shifts of Rossby wave regimes, via the westerly-induced changes in Rossby wave group velocity (Cgx), which are two to three times larger than those in Cpx. We find significant deceleration in the subtropics and polar regions, alongside a salient midlatitude acceleration, of Rossby wave Cgx, especially over the East Asia-Pacific-North America and North Atlantic-Europe sectors. These changes induce robust shifts in spatiotemporal regimes of Rossby waves, from the transient synoptic-scale regime toward the quasi-stationary planetary-scale wave regime where Cgx decelerates, and vice versa. The CESM2 Large Ensemble confirms that the observed pattern over the Eurasia-Pacific-North America sector is a forced response to external forcing, while uncertainties remain over the polar regions and the North Atlantic. We suggest that westerly trends may reshape the regimes of extratropical Rossby wave activity and extreme weather events through the changes in group velocity rather than phase speed of Rossby waves.

title: Contrasting Terminus Dynamics of Lake-Terminating Glaciers in Lago Argentino (Patagonia), 2016–2026: A Training-Free Sentinel-2/Sentinel-1 Workflow
abstract: Lake-terminating glaciers of the Southern Patagonian Icefield are retreating rapidly, yet dense multi-glacier records of their termini remain scarce. We present a training-free workflow in Google Earth Engine that measures ice-area change within a fixed terminus domain from every usable Sentinel-2 scene (per-scene Otsu threshold on the near-infrared band, with cloud screening restricted to lake pixels) and delineates annual terminus positions automatically. Applied to Perito Moreno, Upsala and Spegazzini glaciers (Lago Argentino, Argentina) for October–March 2016–2026, it yielded 260 scenes. Perito Moreno showed no significant trend until mid-2019 and then lost 0.39 km2 a−1 (p < 0.001); its terminus retreated by about 580 m in nine summers; the two most recent summers showed the largest seasonal losses of the record (≈1.6–1.7 km2); and in March 2026 the front detached from Península de Magallanes. Upsala retreated by about 1010 m (≈130 m a−1), whereas Spegazzini remained within ±100 m of its 2017 position. Warm, dry summers in 2021–2022 affected all three glaciers, so their contrasting responses suggest that basin geometry and lateral support modulate the response to a common climate. Sentinel-1 reproduced the Perito Moreno decline but failed in iceberg-choked Brazo Upsala.

title: Ice breakup dynamics on the Kuskokwim River: climatic trends and hydro-meteorological drivers
abstract: River ice breakup is a critical hydrological process governing flood risk and transportation in sub-arctic regions. This study investigates hydroclimatic drivers of breakup timing on the lower Kuskokwim River, Alaska, synthesizing a 102-year observational record (1924–2025) with ERA5 reanalysis. Statistical analysis reveals a winter warming trend driving a phenological advancement of 0.77 days per decade, yet inter-decadal timing variance remains persistently high. Classifying historical events into early, normal, and late categories demonstrate that despite varying spring warming rates, the ice cover consistently requires ∼ 231°C-days of thermal accumulation to reach structural susceptibility. Late breakups are delayed by deep spring snowpacks acting as thermal insulators, not by differing thermal requirements. While atmospheric heat pre-conditions the ice, pre-breakup discharge acts as an independent mechanical trigger. These results provide a categorical framework for tracking warming trajectories and contextualizing extreme events in data-limited basins.

title: Monsoon zonal seesaw: Development of the South Asian monsoon aridified North Africa in the Cenozoic
abstract: North Africa experienced a pronounced transition from humid to arid conditions during the early Cenozoic. Meanwhile, the South Asian monsoon underwent substantial intensification, largely driven by the uplift of the Himalayan-Tibetan Plateau. Here, we demonstrate that the two events, which greatly shaped the paleoenvironment and modern regional climate, are not independent responses to paleogeography changes; rather, the former is primarily driven by the latter through the monsoon-desert mechanism, in which South Asian monsoon diabatic heating produces large-scale subsidence and aridity over North Africa. Using multiple ensembles of paleoclimate simulations and a model for the atmospheric response to imposed diabatic heating, we show that the intensification and poleward shift of Asian monsoon rainfall each make comparable contributions to the aridification of North Africa. Our findings identify a persistent dynamical pathway linking the South Asian and North African monsoons and suggest that it played a major role in early Cenozoic North African aridification, while its climatic expression at other times depended on the relative strengths of competing forcings.

title: SATFRONT: Detecting Atmospheric Fronts with Satellite Data using Machine Learning
abstract: arXiv:2610.42111v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Atmospheric fronts are associated with much of the high-impact weather in the mid-latitudes, yet their identification and classification remain largely manual and subjective. Existing deep learning approaches rely primarily on gridded reanalysis or forecast data, limiting their applicability to satellite observations available for time-critical applications. We introduce SATFRONT, a machine learning framework for detecting cold, warm, and occluded fronts over Europe from geostationary satellite observations, with reanalysis data as an optional additional input. The model is trained on frontal analyses from five European national meteorological services and evaluated against UK Met Office analyses for 2024. Using satellite observations alone, SATFRONT achieves a Critical Success Index (CSI) of 0.428 at a 150 km tolerance, within the range of agreement between analyses from different meteorological services (0.277-0.501) and higher than that of an operational rule-based front detector that uses satellite data (0.133). Adding ERA5 reanalysis increases the CSI to 0.591. ERA5 substantially improves the placement of individual fronts, although its effect on their annual spatial distribution varies by front type. These results demonstrate that cold, warm, and occluded fronts can be detected directly from geostationary satellite observations, providing a basis for automated frontal analyses at the high temporal frequency required for time-critical applications.

title: Impact of temperature variability on mortality during extreme heat and cold conditions over 20 years: A time-space-stratified case-crossover study
abstract: by Yuchen Wei, Fang Guo, Yawen Wang, Zihao Guo, Guozhang Lin, Conglu Li, Shi Zhao, Chao Ren, Kin Fai Ho, Eng Kiong Yeoh, Ka Chun Chong Background Climate change-induced temperature variability poses growing health risks. The effects of this variability on mortality are well established; however, its specific impact during extreme heat and cold conditions remains understudied. This represents a knowledge gap, as the human body’s physiological capacity to adapt to sudden temperature shifts is compromised when ambient temperatures are extreme. To address this, our study examined the relationship between mortality and temperature variability in Hong Kong for a 21-year period. Methods A time-space-stratified case-crossover design was used in this study. Daily weather data from ERA5-Land and PM2.5 levels from ChinaHighPM2.5 were combined with mortality records in Hong Kong from 2000 to 2020. Diurnal temperature range (DTR) and temperature changes between consecutive days (TCN) were used as the temperature variability metrics. Extreme hot and cold conditions were defined by annual temperature percentiles: > 75%, > 90%, > 95%, > 97.5% for hot seasons, and Results DTR and TCN were strongly associated with mortality during heat extremes. For temperatures >97.5th percentile, DTR (odds ratio [OR] = 1.99, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.90-2.08) and TCN (OR = 2.24, 95% CI: 2.09-2.40) showed increased risks for all-cause mortality. During cold extremes ( Conclusion Temperature variability was associated with an increased risk of mortality during extreme heat conditions, with mortality risk rising alongside higher extreme temperature levels, while during extreme cold, the associations were generally smaller. At temperatures above the 97.5th percentile, each 1°C increase in DTR and TCN was associated with approximately 99% and 124% higher odds of all-cause mortality, respectively. These findings highlight the need for targeted public health strategies to protect vulnerable populations from climate-induced temperature fluctuations.

title: Detecting Weather Fronts from Satellite Observations: What Does Reanalysis Add?
abstract: arXiv:2611.08148v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Weather fronts are transition regions between air masses with contrasting thermodynamic properties and are associated with mid-latitude precipitation and severe weather. We investigate machine learning (ML) methods for detecting weather fronts and quantify the contribution of reanalysis data to performance. We compare two configurations of the same ML model for pixel-wise frontal classification over the North Atlantic and Europe: (1) using only geostationary infrared satellite observations, and (2) additionally using 28 ERA5 reanalysis fields. The satellite-only model achieves a neighbourhood critical success index at a 150 km tolerance (CSI@150) of $0.402$, which lies within the range of agreement between analyses from different meteorological services. The satellite$+$ERA5 model achieves $0.575$, an improvement of $0.173$. Our analysis shows that low-level winds are the least predictable from the satellite representation ($R^2 = 0.23$, compared with $0.88$ for temperature), while removing winds or moisture causes the largest decreases in detection performance.

title: Antecedent Snowpack Conditions and Shifting Hydroclimatic Controls on Vegetation Productivity: Implications for Sustainable Watershed Management
abstract: Climate warming is altering seasonal snow regimes and vegetation phenology in cold regions, but the influence of snowmelt may extend well beyond spring thaw. We examined how snow-related associations with net primary productivity (NPP) changed across the growing season in the Naoli River Basin during 2014–2024. Monthly NPP was reconstructed using the Carnegie–Ames–Stanford Approach and evaluated against MODIS NPP. The growing season was divided into early (EGS), peak (PGS), and late (LGS) stages based on vegetation phenology. Generalized additive models identified contemporaneous, lagged, and cumulative associations of air temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, and snow water equivalent (SWE), while random forest and partial dependence analyses were used to compare driver importance and SWE–NPP responses. SWE showed antecedent associations, with AIC-selected April-referenced windows A0L4 (EGS; R2 = 0.23) and A0L3 (LGS; R2 = 0.24). Solar radiation remained the most important predictor, but its relative importance declined from 53.77% in the EGS to 42.56% in the LGS. SWE was more important than precipitation in the EGS (18.96% vs. 12.38%) and PGS (17.31% vs. 13.86%), whereas precipitation became more important in the LGS (19.75% vs. 15.13%). The SWE–NPP relationship also shifted from an overall declining response in the EGS to a nonlinear response in the PGS and a predominantly positive response in the LGS. These results highlight the value of considering antecedent snowpack conditions alongside growing-season climate in vegetation productivity monitoring, with implications for sustainable watershed management under climate change.

title: Forest or tundra? How different vegetation reconstructions of Last Glacial landscapes in Europe may shape our perception of early human dispersal processes
abstract: ABSTRACT Regional variability and long‐term changes of past ecosystems likely had a strong impact on hunter–gatherer population dynamics, including the expansion of anatomically modern humans and the disappearance of Neanderthals. However, our understanding of these ecosystems remains limited, even when looking at large‐scale patterns, such as the extent and distribution of forested areas. Vegetation reconstructions are key to better understanding ecological preferences and their influence on the spatial distribution and dispersals of early humans. Here, we compare four different vegetation reconstruction techniques, two based on pollen data and two vegetation models, between 70 and 20 thousand years before present in Europe. Absolute values in forest cover can differ by up to 40% between reconstruction techniques, highlighting that the choice of method can make the difference between a boreal forest and a tundra. Besides method‐specific and statistical uncertainties, the reason for such a substantial offset lies in the loose definition of forest cover metrics, rendering a direct comparison between methods impossible. At the same time, we show that all reconstruction techniques accurately reconstruct ecosystem dynamics over time on continental to regional scales. We therefore highly recommend that researchers use relative forest cover measures as the more robust method to estimate past landscapes.

title: Value of Adding AI Weather Model Ensembles to a Multi-model Probabilistic Blend
abstract: arXiv:2610.42130v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many weather forecasting organizations use a multi-model blend of ensemble members from different prediction systems to obtain a more accurate forecast. Recent studies have shown that blending deterministic AI-based models alongside physics-based models improves the overall forecast skill. However, the incorporation of an ensemble AI-based model into a multi-model blend is yet to be investigated. This study explores the value of blending the ensemble version of the Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS-CRPS) with the Met Office's convection permitting physics-based ensemble, MOGREPS-UK. We show that blending site temperature (and wind speed) forecasts over the United Kingdom from both ensemble physics-based and ensemble AI-based models leads to an increase in overall forecast skill spatially, across lead times and across exceedance thresholds, especially when the models have different error characteristics. By decomposing the continuous ranked probability score of the blend into component means and diversity terms, we show that a more accurate blend can be achieved by assigning more weight to more skillful models and using models with complementary errors. For example, we show that a blend of MOGREPS-UK with either AIFS-CRPS or the physics-based Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) is better than a blend of IFS and AIFS-CRPS which are not very diverse. This has implications for the importance of weather model diversity and may lend weight to different model development approaches being pursued in tandem. We also demonstrate that calibrating AIFS-CRPS forecasts yields an increase in forecast skill comparable to calibrated ensemble physics-based forecasts, and calibrating the source forecasts before blending and the blended forecast after blending improves the overall forecast accuracy.

title: Stable isotope variability in drip water and its implications for speleothem-based Indian Summer Monsoon reconstruction
abstract: Study region Dandak Cave, located in the Core Monsoon Zone of India. Study focus Understanding the transfer of isotopic composition from precipitation through the karst system to cave drip water is essential for interpreting speleothem-based reconstructions of the Indian Summer Monsoon. Drip water was monitored at three sites in Dandak Cave between 2004 and 2006, with measurements of δ 18 O, δ 13 C, and drip rate conducted to investigate the hydrological and geochemical controls on drip water isotopic composition. The observed drip-water δ 18 O was compared with precipitation δ 18 O estimates from a Rayleigh box model and an isotope-enabled general circulation model ensemble. New hydrological insights for the region Drip water δ 18 O displayed a seasonal cycle, with lower (higher) values during the monsoon (non-monsoon) months, consistent with the seasonal evolution of the estimated precipitation δ 18 O. The relatively small amplitude of drip water δ 18 O compared to that of precipitation suggests attenuation of event-scale variability within the soil–epikarst. Although the three monitoring sites differed in mean drip rate and drip rate variability, their seasonal mean δ 18 O values varied by only 0.1–0.2‰, indicating that they record a similar integrated seasonal signal. δ 13 C varied among sites, reflecting the combined influence of drip hydrology, carbon sources, and cave processes. δ 13 C and radiocarbon analyses yielded limestone-derived carbon contributions of 26 ± 3% and 24 ± 4%, respectively, indicating substantial host-rock carbon input.

title: Rekonstruksi Iklim Purba Miosen Tengah Berdasarkan Studi Palinologi Formasi Lemau Di Seluma, Bengkulu
abstract: AbstrakFosil polen dan spora yang hadir dalam batuan dapat dimanfaatkan untuk merekonstruksi iklim purba saat batuan tersebut diendapkan. Penelitian mengenai iklim purba menggunakan fosil polen dan spora di Pulau Sumatra masih sangat jarang dilakukan. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk merekonstruksi iklim purba pada Miosen Tengah di Seluma, Bengkulu menggunakan fosil polen dan spora dari Formasi Lemau. Pengambilan sampel menggunakan metode purposive sampling dari penampang stratigrafi terukur dengan interval sampel 5-8 cm. Analisis laboratorium menggunakan metode hidrogen peroksida dan penentuan iklim berdasarkan kehadiran fosil Arboreal Pollen, Non Arboreal Pollen, Graminae, Montane Pollen dan spora. Dari 9 sampel yang dianalisis, menunjukkan 4 zona perubahan dengan dominasi 3 zona berupa iklim hangat dan lembab dan 1 zona dengan iklim hangat dan kelembaban sedang (Zona 3). Selain itu berdasarkan perbandingan kehadiran fosil Arboreal Pollen dan Non Arboreal Pollen, Zona 1 dan Zona 3 menunjukkan kondisi vegetasi tertutup dan Zona 2 dan Zona 4 menunjukkan kondisi vegetasi terbuka. Iklim hangat yang terjadi di daerah penelitian sebagai dampak dari adanya peristiwa global Middle Miocene Climate Optimum (MMCO) dan Middle Miocen Climate Transition (MMCT).AbstractPollen and spore fossils present in rocks can be used to reconstruct the paleoclimate when the rocks were deposited. Research on paleoclimate using pollen and spore fossils on Sumatra Island is still very rare. This study aims to reconstruct the paleoclimate in the Middle Miocene in Bengkulu using pollen and spore fossils from the Lemau Formation. Sampling used a purposive sampling method from measured stratigraphic cross-sections with a sample interval of 5-8 cm. Laboratory analysis used the hydrogen peroxide method and climate determination based on the presence of Arboreal Pollen, Non-Arboreal Pollen, Graminae, Montane Pollen and spore fossils. Of the 9 samples analyzed, it shows 4 change zones with a dominance of 3 zones in the form of a warm and humid climate and 1 zone with a warm and moderate humidity climate (Zone 3). In addition, based on the comparison of the presence of Arboreal Pollen and Non-Arboreal Pollen fossils, Zone 1 and Zone 3 show closed vegetation conditions and Zone 2 and Zone 4 show open vegetation conditions. The warm climate that occurred in the research area was the impact of the global events of the Middle Miocene Climate Optimum (MMCO) and Middle Miocene Climate Transition (MMCT).

title: Decadal strengthening of the preceding-winter ENSO influence on subsequent pre-flood-season precipitation over southern China. Part II: Strengthened La Niña teleconnection due to slower decay and enhanced WES feedback
abstract: Abstract In Part I, we documented a marked mid-1990s strengthening of the ENSO influence on pre-flood-season (PFS; April–June) rainfall over southern China (SC) and identified the dominant mechanism for the strengthened El Niño teleconnection. Here we focus on La Niña and examine why its influence on SC PFS rainfall strengthens after the mid-1990s. Observations show that La Niña events during 1996–2021 (P2) exhibit a slower decay than those during 1959–1995 (P1), allowing cold sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies to persist into AMJ over the Niño4 region and more strongly suppressing central-Pacific convection. The resulting Matsuno–Gill response induces more pronounced low-level wind anomalies over the western North Pacific (WNP). Together with intensified wind–evaporation–SST (WES) coupling in P2, these wind anomalies more effectively modulate surface latent heat fluxes and amplify local SST and convection anomalies over the WNP, exciting a stronger cyclonic circulation spanning the South China Sea and WNP. The associated northeasterly anomalies enhance cold–dry advection over SC, favoring anomalous subsidence and reduced moisture supply and thereby intensifying SC rainfall deficits during La Niña decay years in P2. CMIP6 historical simulations provide complementary support: models with a stronger WES coupling show a stronger La Niña–SC PFS linkage. These results show that the strengthened La Niña teleconnection arises from the combined effects of slower La Niña decay and enhanced WES coupling, providing a phase-dependent counterpart to the El Niño mechanism identified in Part I and highlighting the importance of accurately representing ENSO evolution and WNP air–sea coupling in seasonal prediction of SC PFS rainfall.

title: Evaluating the Behavior of 230 Th and 3 He Constant‐Flux Proxies Across a Carbonate Preservation Gradient in the Cocos Ridge
abstract: Abstract We present a comparison of extraterrestrial 3 He ( 3 He ET ) and excess 230 Th ( 230 Th xs ) as constant flux proxies across a depth transect on the Cocos Ridge, evaluating their behavior as a function of carbonate dissolution and lateral sediment redistribution. Overall, 60% of paired 3 He ET ‐ and 230 Th xs ‐derived mass accumulation rate (MAR) estimates overlap within 1σ uncertainty, indicating broad agreement between the two systems. However, statistically significant discordances between He‐ and Th‐derived MARs occur in three of four cores, with He‐derived MARs exceeding Th‐derived MARs at the ridge crest (positive ΔMAR values) and falling below Th‐derived MARs at flank sites (negative ΔMAR). The discordance at the ridge crest is consistent with sediment winnowing and preferential removal of 3 He‐bearing particles, whereas the smaller discordances in flank cores are best explained by a complementary focusing signal, likely reflecting redistribution of material removed from the ridge top. Evaluation of the negative ΔMAR offsets demonstrates that 230 Th xs is effectively retained during carbonate dissolution, as ΔMAR responses remain small despite strong CaCO 3 preservation gradients, and theoretical constraints indicate negligible thorium mobility. When applied jointly, the two proxies provide complementary constraints on MARs that would remain unresolved using a single proxy. However, their interpretation remains site‐dependent, requiring careful consideration of sediment composition, transport regime, and analytical limitations. Because sedimentary burial fluxes are calculated from component concentrations and MAR, these proxy‐dependent differences directly affect estimates of carbonate and other elemental burial fluxes, with implications for reconstructing both past and modern marine biogeochemical cycles.
