title: Early winter underestimated Indian Ocean teleconnections to the Northern extra-tropics in seasonal forecast models
abstract: Abstract There has been increased attention to the Indian Ocean as a source of predictability for the early winter climate over the North Atlantic European (NAE) region in the form of a North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO)-like pattern. Particularly, the October Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) triggers a delayed precipitation response over the Indian Ocean in early winter, which mediates the Rossby wave that propagates to the NAE sector. Seasonal forecast models have been found to be severely underestimating this teleconnection, and finding the underlying causes is crucial to the improvement of the models’ performance. We demonstrate that models lack an adequate December Indian Ocean convective response, both in terms of magnitude and spatial pattern. This misrepresentation of the heating influences the generation of Rossby Wave Source (RWS) along the subtropical jet. Employing a dry linear baroclinic model, we also find that the December upper-tropospheric mean state does not support accurate downstream wave propagation in the forecast models. Particularly, a combination of a stronger subtropical jet and erroneous polar waveguide zonally traps the wave train in the models. Furthermore, our linear model simulations also suggest that this inaccurate downstream wave propagation potentially affects the strengthening of the wave over the North Pacific.

title: Extremes, Teleconnections, and Trends in Growing Season Precipitation over the Corn Belt, 1182–2023 CE
abstract: Abstract Tree-ring chronologies were used to reconstruct growing-season precipitation for the North American Corn Belt from 1182–2023 CE. The reconstruction explains close to 60% of the variance in instrumental May–July precipitation totals (1901–2014) and reproduces the teleconnections with circulation and surface climate variables detected in the instrumental precipitation data, substantiating the skill of the reconstruction and indicating episodic co-occurrence of drought between major crop production regions of the central United States and Eurasia. The episode with five consecutive years of deficit May through July precipitation totals in the Corn Belt from 1930–1934 during the Dust Bowl drought was exceeded by several uninterrupted droughts reconstructed during the pre-instrumental period. The early 17 th century drought (1627–1639) was the most severe, sustained, and unbroken drought in the reconstruction for at least 600-years and has no analog in the modern instrumental observations. This drought coincided with decadal dryness in China and eastern Europe and provides a paleoclimatic example of simultaneous megadrought in major breadbasket regions of Eurasia and North America. The decade of wetness during the early 21 st century in the instrumental observations appears to have been unmatched for 700-years and may have been enhanced by increased humidity and radiation changes associated with the dramatic intensification of agriculture in the Corn Belt.

title: Estimating ensemble-mean anomaly correlations and the ratio of predictable components using an unbiased estimate of the predictable signal variance
abstract: arXiv:2611.07878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The correlation ($r$) between ensemble mean forecasts and observations is a frequently-used metric of forecast quality in the weather and climate prediction communities. However, uncorrected estimates of $r$ are biased towards zero at finite ensemble size due to the influence of unpredictable noise that contaminates the sample ensemble mean. This note summarises established ensemble-size adjustment methods and characterises the behaviour of $r_{\infty}$, a correlation estimator that is constructed from an unbiased and ensemble-size-independent estimate of the signal variance. The only requirement is that forecast members are exchangeable with one another such that they can be interpreted as independent draws from a case-specific predictive distribution. The estimator $r_{\infty}$ does not require forecasts and observations to be statistically exchangeable, only that the unpredictable component of each member is uncorrelated with the observed truth, and thus works for both reliable and unreliable forecasts. In some situations, $r_{\infty}$ may be undefined (i.e. the estimated signal variance is negative) or fall outside the admissible range $-1 \leq r_{\infty} \leq 1$ when the predictable signal is small relative to the sampling uncertainty. These inadmissible values can be interpreted as evidence that the true predictable signal cannot be resolved with the available ensemble size and number of cases. The same unbiased signal variance can also be used to estimate the correlation between the predictable signal and individual members to yield an ensemble-size-invariant estimator of the ratio of predictable components (RPC). In contrast, variance-based RPC estimates, including forms that correct only the model predictable component, are biased low by a factor that depends only on the ensemble size and model signal-to-noise ratio.

title: A Land-Sea Contrast Pattern in Surface Temperature and Atmospheric Circulation Trends in Recent Decades
abstract: arXiv:2606.19581v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We argue land-sea contrast is an important driver of spatial patterns of observed surface temperature and atmospheric circulation trends, including the negative Inter-Decadal Pacific Oscillation (IPO)-like tendency across the Pacific basin. Observed and modeled trends display an overall decline in sea level pressure over the faster-warming land, with a spatial pattern that resembles the seasonal cycle and modeled response to land heating. Coupled historical forcing climate model simulations underestimate the land-sea warming ratio. It is only in the early response of abrupt CO2 quadrupling climate model simulations that climate models are able to recreate the observed land-sea warming ratio, in which case a negative IPO-like sea level pressure trend and surface warming pattern over the Pacific comparable to observed trends are seen. We propose that some discrepancies between observed trends and those predicted by climate models are explained by the underestimation of the land-sea warming ratio by climate models.

title: Unreported mass movement cascades and future Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) hazard in Jammu and Kashmir, Western Himalaya
journal: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
abstract: Abstract. The Warwan sub-basin in Jammu and Kashmir is a remote glaciated region containing several glacial lakes and has recently experienced population growth and infrastructure development. Due to inaccessibility and geomorphic masking, multiple mass movement events including avalanches and Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) have remained largely unreported. This study analyzes three major avalanche events from the past two decades. The September 2005 and September 2020 avalanches originated from glaciers GL-B and GL-A within the same glacier complex, while the March 2020 rock–ice avalanche initiated from the headwall of glacier GL-F in an adjacent valley and terminated before reaching its ablation zone. Runout mapping shows that the September 2020 avalanche descended from the headwall of GL-A and impacted its proglacial lake, triggering a GLOF. In contrast, the September 2005 event terminated before reaching the glacial lake that began forming in 1999 at the terminus of GL-B. Geomorphic analysis indicates persistent sediment influx from meltwater streams of GL-D and GL-E into the lake associated with GL-A, progressively infilling the basin. Continued glacier retreat caused meltwater to accumulate behind the sediment infill, dividing the basin into two disconnected lakes. Impact from the September 2020 avalanche led to complete drainage of stored water and sediment, generating a downstream debris flow. Pre- and post-GLOF imagery reveals breaching and widening of the outflow channel and deposition of a debris fan downstream. The repeated history of mass movements and continued growth of glacial lakes raise serious hazard concerns in the Warwan sub-basin. GLOF modeling identifies Lake-B as potentially hazardous lake at the present condition posing significant downstream risk. Settlements such as Youdu and Qaderna, along with bridges, roads, and residential structures, lie within potential GLOF inundation zones. High sediment availability from past mobilization and deposition along the valley increases the potential of debris flow cascades, posing elevated risks to downstream infrastructure and hydropower, underscoring the need for preparedness and mitigation planning. GLOF modeling suggest that early warning system closer to the source will be able to provide a good lead time in case of potential GLOFs in the valley.

title: Glaciotectonic Spectrum
journal: Transactions of the Kansas Academy of Science
abstract: Glaciotectonic landforms include a spectrum of hill-hole pairs, composite ridges, push moraines, cupola hills, and drumlins with deformed internal structures. Their regional distribution as well as buried glaciotectonic features are reviewed with an emphasis on Scandinavia, adjacent Russia, and Baltic nations. LiDAR and ground investigations were the keys for recognizing murtoos as a new category of distinct glaciotectonic landforms, which are particularly well documented in Finland and Sweden. Three main zones of glacial landscapes are recognized for ice-sheet glaciation - outer, intermediate, and inner, as well as a transitional boundary between the outer and intermediate zones. Glaciotectonic phenomena are numerous and widespread in all of these zones wherever the substratum consists of sedimentary bedrock or unconsolidated sediments.

abstract: Injecting fluids underground for energy projects can trigger earthquakes. Predicting these events is difficult because underground pressure changes slowly, while faults can move in a fraction of a second. We developed a computer method that switches between two ways of calculating these processes. abstract: High-resolution weather models over mountains need terrain smoothing to avoid crashing, but standard methods smooth everywhere regardless of need. We developed Slope-Constrained Orography, a tool that uses one slope-angle setting to adjust only the points that are too steep. Tested over the southeastern Tibetan Plateau, stable simulations were achieved while modifying far less terrain than standard smoothing, offering a simpler approach to running weather models over steep terrain.

title: GECKO-A v1.0: exploring VOC oxidation trajectories through comparison with the master chemical mechanism
abstract: This study presents the first open-source release of a tool that automatically generates chemical mechanisms for the atmospheric oxidation of organic compounds. Simulations for five hydrocarbons, under conditions ranging from urban to remote, are compared with a benchmark mechanism. Results show that describing successive oxidation steps is key to simulating the formation of low-volatility and water-soluble species important for aerosols. A reduced mechanism reproduces most of these results.

title: Identifying Snow-Covered Areas from Unoccupied Aerial Systems (UAS) Visible Imagery and Lidar: A Comparison of Methods
abstract: Visible images from unoccupied aerial systems (UAS) can be used to map snow, especially where snow is shallow and does not last long. We tested several methods for identifying snow-covered areas using UAS images collected in southern New Hampshire, USA. We found that using the full color information gives the most reliable results. We showed how UAS surveys can be planned to create accurate snow cover maps, helping track snow in changing conditions.

title: cSINGV v1.0: development and evaluation of a 1.5 km  coupled atmosphere–ocean–wave modelling  system for the Western Maritime Continent
abstract: Weather over Southeast Asia is shaped by complex interactions between the air, ocean, and waves. We developed a high-resolution model that links these processes to better understand and predict rainfall patterns in the region. The results show that ocean–atmosphere interactions improve the representation and prediction of squall events that affect daily life in Singapore and surrounding regions. This work supports more accurate weather forecasting in the region.

title: A deep-atmosphere extension in a nonhydrostatic dynamical core: formulation and idealized tests
abstract: Many atmospheric models use shallow approximation that work well when the model top is low. As models top now reach higher layers, these approximation need to be relaxed. We develop a deep atmosphere dynamical core(GMCORE), including full deep atmosphere dynamics, and spherical geometry. The tests case with idealized baroclinic waves and tropical cyclones show that the new model reproduces known results and can alter storm trajectory, suggesting value for future high-top and tropical studies.

title: An open-source Python framework for the flexible deployment and advanced applications of the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) model
abstract: Hydrological models help scientists understand water movement and predict changes in water resources. However, their increasing complexity makes them difficult to use. This study developed an open-source framework to simplify the setup and application of the Variable Infiltration Capacity model. Tests in multiple basins showed that the framework improves efficiency, provides reliable simulations, and supports wider use of hydrological models.
